description:
In the heart of Gandava — the old headquarters town of the Jhal Magsi District on the Kachhi (Kach Gandava) plain of Balochistan — stands a *darbar* of the *Sevapanthi* tradition, the order of devotees descended from Bhai Gurdas, the disciple of Guru Gobind Singh who is said to have carried the Nanakpanthi teaching into Sindh and Balochistan in the eighteenth century. According to the anthropologist Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, who has surveyed the Hindu and Sikh heritage of the region, the Gandava darbar was founded by one of Bhai Gurdas's disciples; the *Sevapanthis* (also written Sewapanthis, "those of the path of service") established such darbars and *dharamshalas* in many towns of Sindh and Balochistan, joining the veneration of Guru Nanak to a discipline of charitable hospitality. The Gandava darbar is celebrated above all for its woodwork: an intricately carved wooden frame decorating the main façade depicts Baba Guru Nanak flanked by his companions Bhai Bala and Bhai Mardana, together with the Hindu deities Ganesha (*Ganpati*) and Krishna — a vivid emblem of the syncretic Nanakpanthi devotion in which Sikh and Hindu figures share a single sacred idiom. The carving belongs to the same tradition of craftsmanship that produced the famed woodwork of the Khatwari Darbar at Shikarpur (a separate entry in this dataset), and the wider district is noted for such carvings of Krishna, Ganpati and Guru Nanak with his minstrel companions. Filed here under "Sikh Gurdwara" as the closest of the dataset's three categories, the darbar is more precisely a Nanakpanthi–Sevapanthi shrine of the kind once common among the Hindu mercantile communities of the Sindh–Balochistan borderland. Its exact date of foundation is not securely recorded, and — like many such darbars whose congregations dispersed after 1947 — the details of its present custody and use are uncertain, though the building and its carved façade were reported still standing when documented in recent years. Kalhoro's account also gives Bhai Gurdas's personal history: born Bhai Kanya Lal, he is remembered as a Khalsa saint who received the blessing of Guru Gobind Singh himself before carrying that teaching into the towns of Sindh and Balochistan. Independent confirmation that Gandava possesses a Hindu temple comes from a 2019 Dawn survey of the town's heritage sites, which lists "a Hindu temple" alongside the tombs of Syed Noor Shah Hussaini and Mian Saleh among the settlement's notable structures — though this piece does not itself identify the temple with the Sevapanthi darbar described above, so it stands as corroboration only that such a building exists in the town, not as confirmation of the specific Bhai Gurdas attribution.

## Bibliography
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "Gurus in Shikarpur," *The Friday Times*, 12 January 2018.
- Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro, "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," *Youlin Magazine*, 6 June 2024.
- Sheikh Javed Ali Sindhi, "Heritage: A Refuge and Fort for Ancient Armies," *Dawn*, 22 December 2019.
qa_note: This entry's Sevapanthi/Bhai Gurdas attribution for the Gandava darbar rests on a single author (Zulfiqar Ali Kalhoro) writing across two publications — "Gurus in Shikarpur," The Friday Times, 12 January 2018, and "The Magnificent Khatwari Darbar in Shikarpur," Youlin Magazine, 6 June 2024 — and has not been independently corroborated by a second, unrelated source; an independent Dawn piece (Sheikh Javed Ali Sindhi, "Heritage: A Refuge and Fort for Ancient Armies," 22 December 2019) confirms only that a Hindu temple exists in Gandava, without naming or identifying it as this darbar. Per the research verdict this addition is treated as PARTIAL rather than STRONG: it rests on this single author's reporting and has not yet been corroborated by an independent source specific to the Sevapanthi/Bhai Gurdas identification. Three related conflicts remain unresolved: (1) a companion research file for the sibling entry Khatwari Darbar, Shikarpur, records the same author's later account that "Some believed Bhai Gurdas first preached in Gandava, Balochistan, before Shikarpur," raising an unresolved question of priority between the Gandava and Shikarpur darbars; (2) it is unclear whether the "Sevapanthi darbar" described here (Kalhoro, 2018) and the "Khatwari Darbar of Gandava" (Kalhoro, 2024) are one and the same building — both accounts point to the same town, author, and wood-carving description, but neither source states this explicitly; (3) Wikipedia's uncitable "Sikhism in Sindh" article attaches the Khatwari tradition's founding water-carrier legend to Bhai Kanhaiya, the historical founder of the Sewapanthi sect, while Kalhoro's articles attach the same story to "Bhai Gurdas (alias Kanhiya/Kanya Lal)" — whether these are the same figure is not resolved by any source fetched. None of these conflicts are resolved here, per this archive's standing practice of reporting contradictions rather than silently choosing a side.
